Both distinct crease points P,Q are equidistant from A,C, so their line is the perpendicular bisector of AC and really folds A onto C. In triangle PQK, PK/QK=3 and the angle at Q is acute; in isosceles PCQ it equals CPQ. evidence.uniquenessReview: On the required acute branch, QK=PK/tan(x)=1. The fold relations imply s=AP=PC=QC, hence KC=s-1>0. Expanding s²=9+(s-1)² cancels the square and gives 2s=10, with the unique admissible value s=5. This also uniquely recovers PD=4, BC=9 and BQ=4, so omitted overall width does not leave an answer continuum.

foldRouteAndComplexity.blindAuxiliaryPoint: K=perpendicular foot of P on BC; a different point
foldRouteAndComplexity.foldPropertyJustification: PA=PC, QA=QC and common PQ make APQ and CPQ congruent bySSS, so APQ=CPQ. Since K is on the crease, APK and CPK are congruent bySAS; A-K-C are collinear, so AKP=CKP=90° and AK=CK. Thus the perpendicular-bisector fact can be explained by prior middle-school congruence rather than a higher-grade reflection theorem.
foldRouteAndComplexity.algebra: t²=(9-t)²+9 cancels t² and gives18t=90. No nonlinear system or quadratic formula is required.
foldRouteAndComplexity.restrictionsApplied: The complex-area/perimeter prohibition is not used as an automatic exemption for a segment question. The actual fold deductions, one existing-line intersection, elementary complements and one linear equation were separately checked. The multiple-choice question does not demand elaborate formal-logic justification. Only acute-angle tan definition is evaluated; equal-angle deduction is geometry, not a forbidden identity between trigonometric ratios.
